messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:
Admitting Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course:
A 60-year-old female presented to the emergency room with a sudden onset of severe headache associated with vomiting. On the administration of a CT scan of the brain, subarachnoid hemorrhage was observed, and an aneurysm was suspected. The patient underwent CT cerebral angiogram, and a bilobed anterior communicating artery aneurysm was discovered, projecting anterosuperiorly with a size of 8 x 7 x 5 mm. On the fourth day of ictus, the patient underwent right pterional craniotomy and clipping of the aneurysm. Following surgery, the patient developed right-sided ptosis that advanced to complete right-sided oculomotor nerve paralysis with a dilated and nonreacting pupil. A CT scan of the brain was performed, but no hematoma or infarct was noted. The patient was discharged on the eighth postoperative day and kept under regular follow-up in our outpatient department.

Discharge Condition:
Stable with recovered oculomotor nerve paralysis.

Course of Treatment:
The patient was administered antiedema measures, anticonvulsant, analgesic, and Nimodipine. The medication was continued for a total of 21 days following the ictus.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to follow up with their healthcare provider regularly.

Follow-up Care:
The patient underwent a Magnetic Resonance Imaging scan of the brain with venogram to rule out any infarct or thrombosis of the cavernous sinus after a week of discharge. No abnormalities were noted. The patient came for follow-up on the 61st postoperative day, and her ptosis had fully recovered. A full recovery of the ocular motor nerve paralysis was noted. The patient was advised to continue regular follow-up with their healthcare provider.

Discharge Medications:
Medications are not listed as per case report instructions.

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
The condition chiefly responsible for the admission is a subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm, which was treated by clipping. The postoperative oculomotor palsy is a complication, not the principal diagnosis. It sits in chapter I (circulatory system), category I60 (nontraumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage).

CODE: I60
